lesson_title: Why Is the Chocolate Not Made Where Cocoa Grows?
hook_text: Two African countries grow most of the world's cocoa. So why do their farmers get only a few cents from every chocolate bar?
clip_script: Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire grow about 60 per cent of the world's cocoa. But the factories, the brands and most of the profit are in Europe and America. How did that happen? Go back to 1884. In Berlin, European leaders divided Africa among themselves. Colonies were told to grow crops and dig minerals for export. Railways ran from farms and mines straight to the sea. Factories stayed in Europe. After independence, the pattern stuck. Raw materials sell cheaply, and their prices bounce up and down. Imagine selling coffee to buy a tractor: when the coffee price falls, you sell more and get the same tractor. Meanwhile, the countries that built machines first, in Britain's Industrial Revolution, grew richer. Development gaps are not about who works harder. They come from history, trade and technology. And they can be changed.
visual_style: A cocoa pod split open beside a wrapped chocolate bar with a price tag; a map of Africa being divided by straight lines; railway lines running from mines to ports; a tractor balanced on a scale against sacks of coffee; a steam engine turning.
pacing: Quick opening question, steady explanation, firm ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how colonialism, trade and technology shaped development.
